Since velocity includes direction, the velocity is not constant; its direction changes even though its magnitude is 80 km/h. So the car's speed is 80 km/h but its velocity keeps changing.
exp: Speed = 80 km/h (constant). Velocity changes because direction changes on the bend.
learningOutcome: Applies Motion concepts and equations to solve quantitative or contextual problems.

q: Why can displacement be zero even for a long journey?
ans: Displacement only depends on the starting and ending positions (start-to-end straight line). If a person travels 100 km and returns to the exact starting point (e.g., a round trip), the displacement is zero, even though 100 km was traveled. Distance captures the actual path; displacement captures only net position change.
exp: Displacement = final position - initial position. Round trip → same start/end → displacement=0.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Compare average speed and average velocity. When are they equal?
ans: Average speed = total distance / total time (scalar). Average velocity = net displacement / total time (vector). They are equal in magnitude only when the body moves in one direction along a straight line without reversing (so distance = displacement magnitude).
exp: Avg speed = dist/time; avg velocity = displacement/time. Equal when one-way straight-line motion.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: If you were given a position-time (x-t) graph for an object, how would you find velocity and acceleration?
ans: Velocity = slope (gradient) of the x-t graph at each point = dx/dt. For uniform motion this slope is constant. Acceleration = slope of the velocity-time graph derived from the x-t graph = dv/dt = d²x/dt².
exp: v = slope of x-t graph; a = slope of v-t graph = second derivative of x with respect to t.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: Propose how to measure the acceleration due to gravity using a simple ball-drop experiment.
ans: Drop a ball from rest at a known height h. Measure time t for it to fall. Using s = ½at²: g = 2h/t². Repeat several times and average. Use a ruler for h and a stopwatch or motion sensor for t. Larger h improves accuracy (reduces timing error percentage).
exp: Drop from height h, measure time t. g = 2h/t². Repeat for accuracy.
learningOutcome: Plans, evaluates or reasons about an investigation involving Motion.

q: Why does a ticker-tape timer produce more closely spaced dots when a body moves slowly?
ans: The ticker-tape timer marks dots at regular time intervals (e.g., every 0.02 s). A slow-moving body covers less distance between each dot, so the dots are close together. A fast-moving body covers more distance between dots, so they are further apart. Dot spacing ∝ speed.
exp: Dot spacing = speed × Δt. Low speed → short spacing. High speed → wide spacing.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: What is the difference between a scalar and a vector quantity? Give two examples of each.
ans: Scalar: has only magnitude, no direction (e.g., speed = 60 km/h; distance = 100 m). Vector: has both magnitude and direction (e.g., velocity = 60 km/h north; displacement = 50 m east). You cannot add vectors by simple arithmetic unless they are parallel.
exp: Scalar: magnitude only (speed, distance). Vector: magnitude + direction (velocity, displacement).
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Explain the concept of instantaneous velocity.
ans: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity of an object at a specific instant of time (or at a specific point in its path). Mathematically, it is the limit of Δx/Δt as Δt→0. On a position-time graph, it equals the slope of the tangent at that point.
exp: Instantaneous velocity = velocity at one moment = slope of tangent on x-t graph.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: Why do we say 'average speed' and not just 'speed' for a journey with varying speeds?
ans: When speed varies during a journey, the instantaneous speed changes from moment to moment. Average speed gives a single representative value for the whole trip: total distance / total time. Using just 'speed' would be ambiguous since it changes.
exp: Varying speed → need one representative value for the trip → use average speed = total dist/total time.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: A sprinter runs 100 m in 10 s. Calculate average speed. Can we find average velocity? Explain.
ans: Average speed = 100/10 = 10 m/s. For average velocity, we need displacement. If the 100 m track is straight, displacement = 100 m, so avg velocity = 10 m/s in the forward direction. On a curved track, displacement < 100 m and velocity would be less.
exp: Avg speed = 10 m/s. Avg velocity needs displacement direction. On straight track = 10 m/s forward.
learningOutcome: Applies Motion concepts and equations to solve quantitative or contextual problems.

q: Explain what happens to the velocity of a body in free fall starting from rest.
ans: In free fall starting from rest, the body experiences constant downward acceleration g ≈ 10 m/s². Velocity increases at 10 m/s every second: after 1 s v=10 m/s, after 2 s v=20 m/s, etc. The velocity-time graph is a straight line through the origin with slope g.
exp: Free fall: v increases uniformly. v = gt. After t seconds: v=10t m/s. Linear v-t graph.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: Why does a ball thrown upward keep rising for a time even though gravity acts downward?
ans: The ball has initial upward velocity. Gravity decelerates it at g downward. As long as the upward velocity > 0, the ball keeps moving upward, but slowing down. The ball reaches zero velocity at the highest point, then gravity pulls it back down.
exp: Initial upward v > 0. Gravity decelerates ball. Ball rises until v=0, then falls.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: A driver of a car sees an obstacle 50 m away and brakes. Explain what determines whether the car stops in time.
ans: Stopping distance = thinking distance (v × reaction time) + braking distance (v²/2a). To stop in 50 m, the sum of thinking and braking distances must be ≤ 50 m. Higher speed and lower deceleration increase stopping distance. The deceleration depends on road friction and brake quality.
exp: Stopping dist = reaction dist + braking dist = v×t_reaction + v²/2a. Must be ≤ 50 m.
learningOutcome: Applies Motion concepts and equations to solve quantitative or contextual problems.

q: Why is the concept of relative velocity important in everyday life?
ans: Relative velocity describes how fast one object moves with respect to another. For example, two cars approaching each other at 60 km/h each have relative velocity 120 km/h – they close at twice the speed of either alone. In overtaking, relative velocity is small. This matters for collision safety, navigation, and satellite tracking.
exp: Relative velocity = closing/separating speed. Head-on: v_rel = v1+v2. Same direction: v_rel = v1-v2.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Design a simple experiment to compare the speeds of two toy cars using a ruler and stopwatch.
ans: Set both cars on identical straight tracks of measured length (e.g., 2 m). Start both simultaneously and use a stopwatch to record the time each takes to travel 2 m. Speed = 2 m / time. The car with lower time has greater speed. Repeat 3 times and average for accuracy.
exp: Measure track length, time each car, compare speed = distance/time. Average multiple trials.
learningOutcome: Plans, evaluates or reasons about an investigation involving Motion.

q: Propose how a traffic police radar gun works in terms of the physics of motion.
ans: A radar gun emits radio waves at a known frequency. The waves reflect off the moving vehicle and return. The Doppler effect causes a frequency shift proportional to the vehicle's speed. The gun's electronics measure this shift and calculate speed. It directly measures instantaneous speed using v = c × Δf / (2f), where Δf is frequency shift and c is wave speed.
exp: Radar gun uses Doppler effect: frequency shift of reflected waves ∝ vehicle speed.
learningOutcome: Plans, evaluates or reasons about an investigation involving Motion.

q: What information does a velocity-time graph provide that a distance-time graph does not?
ans: A v-t graph directly shows acceleration (slope = a), the sign of velocity (direction of motion), and displacement (area). A d-t graph shows only speed (slope) and cumulative distance. The v-t graph reveals whether a body is accelerating, decelerating, or at rest, and in which direction, all of which a d-t graph cannot show.
exp: v-t graph: acceleration (slope), displacement (area), direction (sign of v). d-t graph: speed (slope) only.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: Explain the physical meaning of each of the three equations of motion.
ans: 1) v = u + at: final velocity = initial velocity + (acceleration × time). Links velocity and time. 2) s = ut + ½at²: displacement = initial velocity × time + ½ × acceleration × time². Displacement from velocity and time. 3) v² = u² + 2as: relates velocities and displacement without time. Useful when time is unknown.
exp: 1st: v-t relation. 2nd: s-t relation. 3rd: v-s relation (no time needed).
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Why is the distance-time graph for a uniformly accelerating body a parabola?
ans: For uniform acceleration with u=0: s = ½at². This is a quadratic (second-degree) function of t, which means s is proportional to t². When s is plotted against t, the graph is a parabola (not a straight line). The slope (speed) increases linearly as the object accelerates.
exp: s = ½at² is quadratic → s ∝ t² → parabolic d-t graph when body accelerates uniformly.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: Evaluate: 'You can never have a negative displacement.' Is this true?
ans: False. Displacement is a vector. If we define one direction as positive, motion in the opposite direction gives negative displacement. For example, a car moving west when east is defined as positive has negative displacement. Displacement sign depends entirely on the chosen reference direction.
exp: False. Displacement sign depends on reference direction. Motion opposite to positive direction → negative displacement.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: How would the v-t graph of a ball rolling down a ramp and then along a flat floor look?
ans: On the ramp: velocity increases uniformly (positive slope = acceleration due to gravity component). On the flat floor: ball decelerates slowly due to friction (slight negative slope). The graph shows a rising line (ramp), then a nearly horizontal but slightly declining line (flat floor).
exp: Ramp: rising line (acceleration). Flat: shallow declining line (friction deceleration). Two-segment graph.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: What is non-uniform motion? How does it differ from uniform motion?
ans: Non-uniform motion is motion where the speed or direction (or both) change over time – unequal distances are covered in equal time intervals. Uniform motion covers equal distances in equal time intervals at constant speed in a straight line. A car in city traffic is non-uniform; a train at cruising speed on straight track is uniform.
exp: Non-uniform: unequal distances in equal times (variable speed/direction). Uniform: equal distances in equal times.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Explain why a body in uniform circular motion is said to be in non-uniform motion according to one definition but uniform motion according to another.
ans: In UCM, speed (magnitude of velocity) is constant, so it fits the 'equal distances in equal times' definition of uniform. However, the direction changes continuously, so velocity (the vector) is non-uniform. The NCERT definition of uniform motion requires both constant speed AND direction, so UCM is non-uniform by that definition.
exp: UCM: constant speed (=uniform speed) but changing direction (=non-uniform velocity). Per NCERT uniform requires constant velocity → UCM is non-uniform.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: A sprinter at 10 m/s sees the finish line 40 m away. If decelerating at 2 m/s², do they finish?
ans: Using v²=u²+2as: 0=100-4s → s=25 m to stop. Since 25 m < 40 m, the sprinter stops before the finish line. They would not complete the race at this deceleration and would need to keep pushing.
exp: s_stop = u²/(2a) = 100/4 = 25 m < 40 m → sprinter stops 15 m short of finish line.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Explain the significance of the sign of velocity in a one-dimensional motion problem.
ans: In one-dimensional motion, we choose a positive direction. Positive velocity means motion in that direction; negative velocity means motion in the opposite direction. This convention allows a single equation to describe both forward and reverse motion without worrying about direction separately.
exp: Positive v = motion in chosen +ve direction. Negative v = motion in opposite direction. Simplifies equations.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: A car moves at constant velocity for half the time, then at twice that velocity for the rest. Find the ratio of distance covered in each half.
ans: Let velocity = v for time t. Distance1 = v×t. Distance2 = 2v×t. Ratio = 1:2. The second half covers twice as much distance in the same time because speed doubles.
exp: d1 = vt, d2 = 2vt → ratio d1:d2 = 1:2.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Suggest how satellites can use equations of motion to maintain orbit (simplified).
ans: Satellites orbit due to centripetal acceleration provided by gravity. While the three kinematic equations don't directly apply (circular motion), the concepts of velocity, acceleration, and displacement are fundamental. Mission controllers use g = v²/r to find required orbital velocity v = √(gr) for a given radius r, ensuring the satellite's curved fall matches Earth's curvature.
exp: Orbital mechanics: centripetal a = g = v²/r → v = √(gr). Equations adapted for circular/orbital motion.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: What is the meaning of 'rate of change' in the context of motion?
ans: Rate of change means how much a quantity changes per unit time. In motion: speed = rate of change of distance (Δd/Δt); velocity = rate of change of displacement (Δx/Δt); acceleration = rate of change of velocity (Δv/Δt). Faster rate = larger value of the quantity.
exp: Rate of change = change per unit time. Speed = Δd/Δt; velocity = Δx/Δt; acceleration = Δv/Δt.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Compare the d-t graphs of two cars: one at constant 20 m/s and one accelerating from rest at 2 m/s². Which eventually has greater slope?
ans: Car 1: d-t graph is a straight line (constant slope = 20 m/s). Car 2: d-t graph is a parabola with increasing slope (speed = 2t m/s, so slope increases with time). Car 2's slope (speed) = 20 m/s at t=10 s, and exceeds 20 m/s after that. So initially Car 1 has greater slope, but eventually Car 2 wins.
exp: Car1: straight line, slope=20. Car2: parabola, slope increases. Car2 slope > 20 after t=10 s.
learningOutcome: Interprets graphs, representations or data related to Motion and draws conclusions.

q: A car and a bicycle start from rest on the same straight road. Car: a=4 m/s². Bicycle: a=1 m/s². When is the car 90 m ahead?
ans: Position difference = ½×4×t² - ½×1×t² = ½×3×t² = 1.5t². Set equal to 90: 1.5t²=90 → t²=60 → t=√60 ≈ 7.75 s.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

q: Why is it harder to stop a car at higher speeds, even with the same braking force?
ans: Stopping distance = v²/(2a). Since stopping distance depends on v², doubling the speed quadruples the stopping distance. Higher speed means more kinetic energy (½mv²) must be dissipated by the brakes. With the same braking force (same a), a faster car needs much more distance to stop.
exp: Stopping dist = v²/2a ∝ v². Double speed → 4× stopping distance. More KE to dissipate.
learningOutcome: Explains phenomena and gives scientific reasoning using Motion concepts.

(b) Find the retardation during the last 4 s. (c) Sketch the velocity–time graph and use it to determine the total distance travelled.
